Householder
hous'hōld-ēr
n. (the master of a house; the head of a family or estate; the standing figure of God in the kingdom parables)
English household and -er. The Greek oikodespotes is literally the house-despot — the man with undisputed authority over his own estate.

Biblical Definition

The householder is one of the Lord's recurring figures for God Himself, and every parable that uses him turns on his right to do as he will with his own. The servants of the householder come asking about the tares: “Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares?” (Mat 13:27) — and he forbids the uprooting until harvest. Every scribe instructed unto the kingdom “is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” (Mat 13:52) — the faithful teacher holds the Old Testament and the New together and produces both. The householder of Matthew 20:1 “went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard”, and pays the eleventh-hour man a penny, and answers the murmurers, Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? And the householder of Matthew 21:33 plants a vineyard, hedges it, digs a winepress, builds a tower, lets it out to husbandmen, and goes into a far country — and at last sends his son. Four parables, one figure: an owner with absolute right, whose dealings are always just and frequently more generous than his servants think proper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a householder as the master or head of a family; one who keeps house with his family; an occupier of a house.

expand to see more

HOUSEHOLDER, n. The master or head of a family; one who keeps house with his family.

2. An occupier of a house.

The kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder. Matt. xx.

Key Scripture

Mat 13:52 — "Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old."

Mat 20:1 — "For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard."

Mat 20:15 — "Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?"

Modern Corruption

The parable of the labourers is regularly read as a lesson in fair wages, when its subject is the absolute freedom of God to be generous, and the murmuring it exposes is the murmuring of the long-serving.

expand to see more

Matthew 20 is read at cross purposes about as often as any parable in the Gospels. Some read it as an economic teaching about equal pay; others read it as evidence that the householder is unfair, and try to soften him. The parable answers both in verse 15, which is the sentence everything else is built to deliver: Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? No one was underpaid — the first-hired agreed with him for a penny and received a penny. The offence was not injustice but generosity to somebody else, and the parable is a precise description of the human heart, which can bear a loss more easily than it can bear another man's undeserved gain. Paul makes the same argument doctrinally in Romans 9 with the potter and the clay, and the objection he anticipates is exactly the murmuring of Matthew 20. This is the confessional doctrine of unconditional election in parable form: God has mercy on whom He will have mercy, and nobody is wronged. It is also a pastoral warning aimed squarely at the long-serving — the elder brother, the labourer who bore the burden and heat of the day, the man who has been in the church forty years and cannot rejoice over a deathbed conversion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek oikodespotes (G3617), the master of a house; oikos (G3624), a house or household; oikonomos (G3623), the steward set under him.

expand to see more

Greek oikodespotes (G3617) — the master of the house, the head of an estate; the standing figure for God in the kingdom parables; Matthew 13:27, 20:1, 21:33.

Greek oikos (G3624) — a house, and by extension a household or family line; the house of God which is the church; 1 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 3:6.

Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward; the servant who administers what the householder owns and answers for it; Luke 16:1, 1 Corinthians 4:2.

Usage

"“Bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” — the instructed scribe holding both Testaments."

"“Went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard” — the parable of the penny."

"“Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — the question that exposes the murmuring of the long-serving."
